artworks.title: The Goat Amalthea with the Infant Jupiter and a Faun
artworks.description: Bernini's early Borghese marble presents Amalthea as the goat herself: the infant Jupiter and a faun drink at her udder — the Cretan nurse of Zeus carved before the sculptor's fame.

artworks.title: The Infant Jupiter Suckled by the Goat Amalthea
artworks.description: Jordaens' Flemish pastoral fills the Cretan cave with satyrs and the nursing goat — Amalthea as the living source of the hidden god's strength.

artworks.title: The Infant Jupiter Nurtured by the Goat Amalthea
artworks.description: Poussin's classical landscape seats nymphs and the goat around the infant Jupiter — Amalthea's milk as the quiet opening of Olympian power.

artworks.title: Amalthea Nursing the Infant Zeus
artworks.description: A nineteenth-century French painting returns Amalthea to nymph form: the Cretan nurse offers her breast to the hidden child — the tradition in which she is woman, not goat.

popCulture.title: Cornucopia
popCulture.description: The broken horn of Amalthea's goat became the horn of plenty — so the Cretan nurse's gift still names every Western emblem of abundance.

popCulture.title: Amalthea (mythology)
popCulture.description: The foster-mother of Zeus — nymph or goat — who hid and nursed the infant god in Crete until he could overthrow Cronus.
